After hatching, the nascent oozoid of the salp Ihlea punctata measures a mere 0.35 centimeters [Lb = 0.35 centimeters] in length at birth. At a stable water temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], the period between syngamy and the emergence of the first free-swimming feeding stage is completed within a single day (1 day) [ab = 1 day]. This remarkably brief incubation, lasting roughly 24 hours, is characteristic of salps which produce brooded embryos that develop rapidly within the parent blastozooid. The newly released oozoids, although diminutive, are already capable of filter feeding and begin to grow almost immediately, pumping water through their transparent, barrel-shaped bodies to capture phytoplankton. This initial size is notably small compared to the dimensions the solitary oozooid will eventually attain, and reflects a life history strategy centered on rapid generation times and high population turnover in productive oceanic waters.

Field surveys tracking the solitary oozoid generation of Ihlea punctata have revealed considerable somatic growth, with individuals reaching an ultimate oozoid length of 2.2 centimeters [Li = 2.2 centimeters]. This asymptotic size was confirmed by sampling that documented a plateau in growth increments once individuals surpassed a body length of roughly 1.5 centimeters, after which further elongation became negligible. The ontogenetic trajectory toward this maximum size is tightly coupled with the onset of reproductive function; puberty, defined here as the size at which the oozoid begins strobilating to produce blastozooids, occurs when the individual attains a length of 1.1 centimeters [Lp = 1.1 centimeters]. This value was estimated by applying the proportional relationship between length at maturity and ultimate length observed in the better-studied congener Cyclosalpa bakeri, which suggests that I. punctata reaches functional maturity at approximately half its maximal body size. The progression from a few millimeters at birth to over two centimeters represents a substantial volume increase, supported by high filtration rates.

The maximum recorded wet weight for a mature solitary oozoid of Ihlea punctata is 0.22 grams [Wwi = 0.22 grams], a figure derived from volumetric calculations based on the characteristic cylindrical body shape of salps, using a length-volume allometry established for Cyclosalpa bakeri and applied to the species' ultimate length. Such a low body mass relative to length underscores the gelatinous nature of the animal; like other thaliaceans, I. punctata is composed largely of a watery, transparent tunic with minimal structural protein. This modest biomass has direct implications for its trophic ecology. As a gelatiovore, it efficiently harvests nanoplankton but stores very little metabolic reserve, necessitating near-continuous feeding. The ultimate wet weight of 0.22 grams defines the maximum energy reservoir available for reproduction and the metabolic ceiling for the solitary generation, with energetic surplus being channeled directly into the production of successive generations of blastozooids.

Reproductive output in Ihlea punctata has been assessed in the laboratory at a controlled temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], with the solitary oozoid producing a chain of blastozooids at an average frequency of approximately 6.6 events per day [F_R_i = approximately 6.6 events per day]. Each strobilation event liberates a single, functional blastozooid per year [F_R_i = strobilation event liberates a single, functional blastozooid per year], which itself is an aggregate of multiple zooids. This yields a maximum daily reproduction rate of roughly 6.6 new blastozooid chains generated per oozoid each day, a prodigious output that enables rapid population buildup under favorable conditions. The fecundity of this species is therefore not expressed as a discrete clutch or brood in the traditional sense, but as a continuous, near-steady stream of asexually produced offspring. This high-frequency, low-investment per-offspring strategy is typical of opportunistic planktonic grazers that capitalize on ephemeral phytoplankton blooms.

The complete lifespan from birth to the eventual death of the solitary oozoid is constrained to a brief 20 days [am = 20 days] when individuals are maintained at a constant 22.5 °C at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. This compressed schedule means that an oozoid born at dawn will have reached puberty, strobilated to produce new blastozooids, senesced, and expired before the end of the third week. Senescence in this species is rapid and catastrophic, characterized by a loss of turgor and disintegration of the gelatinous body wall. The single-day age at birth (1 day) [ab = 1 day] and the 20-day lifespan (20 days) [am = 20 days] at the same temperature illustrate an extreme pace of life: embryonic development is essentially instantaneous, and the entire adult reproductive window is compressed into a matter of days at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C] at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. This pattern is emblematic of r-selected pelagic invertebrates that rely on high fecundity and rapid maturation rather than longevity to maintain population stability in a variable ocean.
